newsitem.title: JAPAN: Dollar tops 115 yen and Tokyo shares plunge.
newsitem.headline: Dollar tops 115 yen and Tokyo shares plunge.

text.p: The dollar topped 115 yen for the first time in 44 months on Thursday, sparking a selloff of Tokyo stocks that pushed a key index below 19,000, its lowest level in more than a year.

Worries about new financial failures, government economic policy and technical factors ahead of next week's holidays in Japan combined to send the stock and currency markets on twin roller coaster rides.
After a quiet opening, the dollar rose above 115 yen in morning trading, pushing already weak Tokyo stock prices lower.
On the stock market, the benchmark Nikkei average of 225 leading shares plummetted more than 700 points at one stage, but clawed back to end the day down 257.83 points or 1.32 percent at 19,291.58.

The dollar reached as high as 115.12 yen before slipping back below 115 yen later in the day after a senior Finance Ministry official said Japan "does not welcome wild fluctuations in foreign exchange rates".
Dealers said heavy commercial purchases at the morning local fixing were the direct cause of the dollar's rise, but added that the Nikkei's slide accelerated it.

"There had been a substantial amount of Japanese importer purchases at the local fixing (at 0100 GMT) and then we had the fall of stock prices on top of that," said Hank Note, chief dealer with Sumitomo Bank.
But the damage had already been done to stocks, with the benchmark Nikkei immediately falling from Wednesday's close of 19,549.41 points.
By midday, shares were reeling 2.3 percent lower and the plunge continued in the afternoon with the Nikkei falling as low as 18,819.92 in mid-afternoon trade before a late recovery.

Sentiment was also hurt by worries about Japan's financial system. On Wednesday, Yamaichi Securities, one of the nation's biggest brokerages, announced it would spend 150 billion yen ($1.31 billion) to help bail out a subsidiary struggling with unrecoverable real estate loans.
That was followed on Thursday by an announcement by non-bank lender Koei Corp that it would seek liquidation under court protection with debts of about 260 billion yen ($2.28 billion).
Recent weakness in stock prices has strengthened the view that Japan will be forced to keep its interest rates at record lows, hurting sentiment towards the yen and giving the dollar support.
The Nikkei initially dipped due to selling linked to futures trading, brokers said.
"Since we don't know what will happen during the long holiday, some traders closed their positions in the morning," one broker said. The market will be closed from next Tuesday until January 5.

Although Tokyo stocks rebounded on Wednesday, they have been battered since last week by worries about the effects on the economy of the government's tightening of fiscal policy to tackle Japan's budget deficit.
The government has decided to end special income tax cuts from January and raise the consumption tax next April, sparking fears in the market that a fledgling recovery in the economy may be damaged.

Market players were also disappointed with a state budget for the year starting next April, approved by the cabinet on Wednesday, as there is a possibility it will increase the budget deficit, said Yoshiki Hamada, deputy manager of foreign exchange at Asahi Bank.
